title: Choose life (Deuteronomy 30:15–20)
hook: I set before you life and death: choose life
carry: near, in your mouth and in your heart

segments.voice: Yesterday: manna, and a hunger that taught a lesson: not by bread alone. Your line: carried, even when it didn't feel like it.
screen: `CARRIED, EVEN WHEN IT DIDN'T FEEL LIKE IT.`

segments.voice: Plenty of the choices that shape a life don't feel like choices at all. They feel like Tuesday. Text back, or let it slide. Bed, or one more episode. The true thing, or the easy one. Each one is tiny, but laid end to end, they become a direction. Moses is near the end of his great speech in Deuteronomy. Now he boils it all down to a single choice, and sets it in front of his people like two plates on a table.
screen: `CHOICES THAT FEEL LIKE TUESDAY.` → `END TO END, A DIRECTION.` → `TWO PLATES ON A TABLE.`

segments.voice: Here's how Moses says it, in the King James Bible: "See, I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil." A few verses on, he calls witnesses: "I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live." In Hebrew: u-vacharta ba-chayyim, and you shall choose life. Chayyim, life, is plural in form, and some readers hear in that plural that life is always more than one thing: breath and family and land and God, all at once. It's the same word as in the Jewish toast, l'chaim, to life. Notice what Moses doesn't do. He doesn't choose for them. He sets it out, and he pleads. And just before this, he says how possible it is. It isn't too hard for you, or far away, up in heaven or across the sea. "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." Then Moses says what life is: loving God, listening to his voice, holding on to him, "for he is thy life, and the length of thy days." Paul quotes the word is nigh thee in his letter to the Romans, and some Christian readers hear an echo of the two ways in Jesus' words about two roads, one narrow. And notice how often Moses says this day. The choice isn't saved for the end. It's on the table today.
screen: `LIFE AND GOOD, DEATH AND EVIL.` · `CHAYYIM: LIFE, ALWAYS PLURAL.` · `THE WORD IS VERY NIGH UNTO THEE.` · `FOR HE IS THY LIFE.` · then, large: `THEREFORE CHOOSE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Think ahead through the rest of your day and find one small fork, two plates on the table, where one choice leaves you or someone else a little more alive: a walk instead of the scroll, the kind answer instead of the clever one. Picture yourself choosing life there. If you pray, ask for help to choose it.
Choose life. Moses' plea near the end of Deuteronomy: life and death are set before you, and the word is near, in your mouth and in your heart.
Your line: near, in your mouth and in your heart. Two plates, and the choosing is yours. Day four hundred eight, done.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Deuteronomy 30 when speaking about daily decisions and moral choices, and Paul quotes 'the word is nigh thee' from this chapter in Romans 10.

notes: Editor review (y2 days 407–424): hook no longer opens with a "most choices" claim; Deuteronomy 30 called a plea near the end of the speech, not Moses' "final" or "very end" (chapters 31–33 follow); cut the wrong claim that the Hebrew is "even more compact" than two English words; chayyim's plural offered as "some readers hear", not narrator fact; "Christians have heard echoes all through the New Testament" narrowed to what is cited; "calling your mother" swapped for a neutral example; howItsDone "often" removed.

'Chayyim is plural, as if life were always more than one thing': the plural form is grammatical fact; the interpretation is offered lightly ('as if'). Confirm it doesn't read as a preacher's etymology.
Phrase 'choose life' has modern political uses; the script stays with the text. Keeper may wish to note this.
